title: When 12% a year is not 12%
hook: Two accounts both say 12% a year. One pays more. How?

doesNotKnow: that how often interest is added changes what a quoted yearly rate really pays
that the effect grows a little and then levels off

misconception: 12% a year compounded monthly means exactly 12% after a year.
objective: The learner can explain that a quoted rate added in parts during the year pays slightly more than the quoted rate because each part earns interest on earlier parts, and that more frequent adding helps less and less.

claims.text: 12% a year added as 1% each month turns $100 into about $112.68 after a year.
Added yearly, quarterly, monthly or daily, a quoted 12% gives effective rates of 12.00%, 12.55%, 12.68% and 12.75%.
The extra over plain 12% is interest on interest: each month's 1% is taken on a balance that already includes earlier interest.
claims.source: Month k adds 1% of 100 × 1.01^(k−1), which exceeds $1 for k ≥ 2; the sum of the excess is 12.6825 − 12 = 0.6825.

claims.text: Adding interest more often helps less and less: even continuously, 12% a year gives only about 12.75%.
Names vary: APR is often the quoted rate and APY or AER the effective one.
claims.source: US Truth in Savings Act (Regulation DD) defines Annual Percentage Yield as the effective annual rate on deposits; UK uses AER. Usage of 'APR' differs by product (for loans it includes some fees). Brief asks to say 'quoted rate vs effective rate'.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: one deposit, no fees, a 365-day year, the rate held fixed.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation, shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

recall.question: Account A pays 6% a year added once a year. Account B quotes 6% a year added monthly. After a year, which has grown more?
recall.why: B adds 0.5% each month, and later months earn interest on earlier interest, so its effective rate is a little above 6% (about 6.17%). It is a small edge, not a doubling.
